articles.title: Intel stock falls as TSMC eyes Elon Musk's Terafab venture - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Intel stock falls as TSMC eyes Elon Musk's Terafab venture  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
Intel stock fell more than 4% in premarket trading on Monday after Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk confirmed that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. could take part in his Terafab chip manufacturing venture in Texas — a project Intel had been first to support.
TSMC stock rose about 3% in Taiwan and was up 1% in premarket U.S. trading. The development rattled some Intel investors, who see TSMC's possible involvement as a competitive threat, given that Intel had been the earliest backer of Terafab when it pledged its support in April, according to MarketWatch.
Terafab is a joint venture between SpaceX and Tesla to manufacture chips for both companies at a site in Grimes County, Texas. Tesla and SpaceX announced the project with an initial investment of $16.8 billion and a planned workforce of at least 3,000 people. SpaceX said the chips produced there will be used in Tesla's Optimus robots and Cybercabs, as well as in space-based data centers the company is developing. Total spending across all phases could reach as much as $119 billion, the company has said.
Intel had acknowledged a role in the project but has not offered details about what that involvement entails.
TSMC's potential entry into Terafab comes as the Taiwanese chipmaker has been weighing a broader expansion of its U.S. footprint. TSMC is considering construction of a new Texas campus separate from the $265 billion it has already committed to an Arizona campus, with each fabrication plant carrying a price tag of at least $20 billion. Planning for a Texas facility remains in early phases, and TSMC has declined to comment on the matter.
Customers based in North America account for more than 75% of TSMC's wafer revenue this year. TSMC already handles a portion of Tesla's chip manufacturing needs, with Tesla having signed a separate $16.5 billion deal with Samsung for its next-generation AI6 chip, according to Electrek.
Musk has been building out the supplier base for Terafab on multiple fronts. He spoke at ASML's annual technology conference earlier this year, making the case for the project to employees of the Dutch company — the sole supplier of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, which are central to Terafab's planned operations. TSMC, Samsung, and Intel all rely on ASML equipment to fabricate cutting-edge AI chips.

Italy has cleared the financing framework for Silicon Box’s planned semiconductor manufacturing facility in Novara, marking a major step in the country’s strategy to strengthen its position in Europe’s semiconductor industry. The project, known as the Vulcan Project, involves a total investment of €3.2 billion, equivalent to roughly $3.7 billion, with the Italian government providing €1.3 billion (US$1.45 billion) in public support through the semiconductor sector fund established under the European Chips Act.
The project will establish Silicon Box’s first European manufacturing facility and is expected to focus on the back-end stages of semiconductor production, particularly chiplet integration, advanced packaging and testing. A strategic investment in semiconductor manufacturing
The Silicon Box investment in Novara, Italy, represents a €3.2 billion strategic project aimed at strengthening Europe’s semiconductor supply chain. The facility is expected to become Silicon Box’s first European manufacturing site and is projected to create around 1,600 direct jobs at full capacity.
The project focuses on advanced chiplet integration, packaging and testing, technologies increasingly important for artificial intelligence, data centres, electric and autonomous vehicles, telecommunications and high-performance computing. The European Commission granted the facility Open EU Foundry status in March 2026, with full production capacity expected by 2033.
For Italy, the investment supports a broader semiconductor strategy. The country has a multibillion-euro Chips Fund, more than €1 billion committed to EU microelectronics IPCEI projects, and a €225 million (US$252 billion) semiconductor-design centre in Pavia. The project aligns with the EU Chips Act, which aims to mobilise over €100 billion (US$112.1 billion) in policy-driven investment and raise Europe’s semiconductor market share from about 10% to 20% by 2030.
Focus on advanced packaging and chiplets
Silicon Box’s Novara project is significant because it targets the “back-end” of semiconductor production, an area increasingly important as conventional chip scaling becomes more difficult. Instead of producing one large chip, chiplet architecture divides computing functions into smaller components that can be integrated within a single package. This enables manufacturers to combine different technologies and potentially reduce design and production costs.
The technology is particularly relevant to the rapid growth of AI and data-centre computing. The Semiconductor Industry Association estimates that the HBM market alone could reach $21 billion in 2025, reflecting the growing need for advanced memory and packaging solutions in AI systems.
The investment is also notable because Italy identified €4 billion in resources for its national microelectronics strategy, covering investment attraction, research and industrial development. Consequently, Novara could support Europe in developing capabilities beyond traditional wafer fabrication, particularly for AI, high-performance computing and next-generation automotive electronics.

articles.title: High Commissioner Türk: The clock on AI regulation is ticking - ohchr
articles.summary: High Commissioner Türk: The clock on AI regulation is ticking  ohchr
articles.full_text:
Delivered by
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk
At
AI and Human Rights Summit
Dear participants, colleagues, and friends,
I welcome the opportunity to address this important AI and Human Rights Summit, which is focused on how to make sure human ingenuity is in step with human rights.
The ruthless race for AI and the competition that we see have brought us into uncharted waters, with mounting concerns about human agency, our safety, and even our continued existence as a species.
AI has the potential to deliver head-spinning advances across science, education, healthcare, agriculture, public services – and human rights. AI agents can improve our work, organize our days, and take over routine tasks. They can actually also help us give aspiration to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and how we can ensure that it’s implemented.
But, as we all know too well, great power demands responsibility on the same scale. When the two don’t match, we have a problem.
Today’s powerful technological tools are not only being developed and controlled by a select few, without public oversight; they are already doing things that even their creators cannot fully predict or manage.
Accidental failures – let alone deliberate misuse – pose unprecedented threats to virtually every aspect of our lives.
AI can undermine equality, freedom, privacy, and public debate in a million subtle, sophisticated ways – letting dystopia creep in unnoticed.
Entire populations could be cut off from communication, clean water, heating, and financial services at the click of a button. AI is already changing the face of warfare. We need urgent action to prohibit machines from deciding who lives and who dies.
Studies are warning of the cognitive costs of AI for students – from poorer knowledge retention to less independent, less creative thinking. Are we heading towards a future in which no one is able to understand, question, or guide this technology?
Those risks are widely acknowledged, as is the need to mitigate them – even by AI leaders themselves. Yet too few are walking the talk.
Three weeks ago, I wrote to States and frontier AI companies, urging them to take the steps within their control to reduce risks – now.
We need to mobilize – across borders and sectors – to ensure that technology serves humanity, not the other way round. And human rights need to be our compass, our guide, our direction.
We need mandatory human rights safeguards and due diligence in the development and deployment of AI, continuously adapted as the technology evolves.
Countries hosting AI companies and those with influence over their supply chains have a particular obligation to require those companies to act responsibly – and to hold them accountable when they do not.
Not every answer will be found in the laws we already have; some areas will require new legal approaches. But updating existing frameworks – on liability, on cybersecurity, on data protection, and more – can offer protection while more ambitious legislation is developed.
We also need much stronger collaboration on security and independent monitoring within the industry – not in words, but in practice.
Expanding public AI research capacity and ensuring the participation of civil society and those whose rights are affected in decision-making can help steer AI development in the right direction.
We can no longer afford to wait or rely on goodwill. No country and no company can – or should – define the future of AI and people’s rights alone. That is why international cooperation – championed by this Summit – is critical.
There has been some positive momentum, which we need to leverage.
This includes the establishment of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance and the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, as well as the launch of a joint call for stronger control over frontier AI models, supported by 29 States and the European Union.
Last week, AI industry leaders also took new steps to strengthen safeguards, self-regulation, and risk assessment.
The hosts and participants of this summit have themselves been at the forefront of these efforts, spearheading the search for ways to embed human rights firmly in AI governance.
The clock on AI regulation is ticking. If we fail to move quickly, we risk unforeseeable consequences – for ourselves and future generations.
I wish you a productive meeting and look forward to hearing about its outcomes.

articles.summary: ‘The clock on AI regulation is ticking’, warns UN rights chief  UN News
articles.full_text:
The world is running out of time to put guardrails on artificial intelligence, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk warned Monday, as a “ruthless race” between companies and countries raises concerns about human safety and even humanity’s survival.
Speaking in the UK at an AI and Human Rights Summit in Oxford on Monday, Mr. Türk said the technology could deliver dazzling advances in science, health, education – and even human rights work.
But its tools are being built and controlled by a select few, without public oversight, and are already doing things their creators cannot fully predict or manage.
Dystopia-creep
He warned that AI could undermine equality, freedom, privacy and public debate in subtle ways, “letting dystopia creep in unnoticed”. Entire populations could be cut off from communication, clean water, heating and financial services “at the click of a button”.
He called for urgent action to prohibit machines from deciding who lives and who dies, noting that AI is already changing the face of warfare.
He also cited studies showing students who rely on AI retain less and think less independently, and asked whether the world is heading for a future in which no one can understand, question or even guide the technology.
As the UN rights chief was addressing the summit in the UK, New York City Council - home to the financial heart of the US economy - was also holding a rare Committee of the Whole to examine AI risks to New Yorkers.
The council is considering 10 bills to regulate AI across the nation's largest city, with testimony from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta.
Mandatory safeguards
Mr. Türk called for mandatory human rights safeguards and due diligence in how AI is developed and used, adapted as the technology evolves. Countries that host AI companies, or have influence over their supply chains, must require them to act responsibly and hold them to account when they do not, he said.
Not every answer lies in existing law and some areas will need new legal approaches, he added. But updating rules on liability, cybersecurity and data protection could offer protection in the meantime.
He also urged stronger collaboration on security and independent monitoring within the industry – “not in words, but in practice” – and a bigger say for civil society and people whose rights are affected.
“We can no longer afford to wait or rely on goodwill,” he said.
Some momentum
Mr. Türk welcomed the creation of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance and the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI – both UN initiatives – along with a joint call for tighter control of frontier AI models backed by 29 States and the European Union.
He also said AI industry leaders had taken new steps last week on safeguards, self-regulation and risk assessment – apparently a reference to a voluntary accord signed at the White House on 29 September by President Donald Trump and the heads of six AI companies.
It carries no penalties for firms that ignore it, with President Trump describing it as “morally binding”.
‘Walk the talk’
“Too few are walking the talk”, said the rights chief, who wrote to States and frontier AI companies three weeks ago urging them to act now to reduce risks.
“If we fail to move quickly, we risk unforeseeable consequences – for ourselves and future generations,” he said.

articles.title: Monday Morning Moan - California’s leading, not dreaming, when it comes to a grown-up stance on AI regulation. Why can’t frontier model leaders get behind their home state? - Diginomica
articles.summary: Monday Morning Moan - California’s leading, not dreaming, when it comes to a grown-up stance on AI regulation. Why can’t frontier model leaders get behind their home state?  Diginomica
articles.full_text:
We have to do a lot more in the absence of Federal leadership.
That was one of the less colorful comments from Gavin Newsom, Governor of California, the home state to the US tech sector, when asked about the increasingly febrile question of AI regulation, or rather the lack thereof.
He was rather less temperate in his remarks about Donald Trump’s ludicrous attempt to re-brand AI as Super Intelligence in a bid to calm down the calls from within the AI sector itself to slow down the pace of innovation while we all have a little think to take on board some of the safety implications, and maybe come up with some ideas around how not to have the bots kill us all off by 2030 as appears to be the accepted course of events at the moment.
On the decision by the President of the Unites States (sic) to take time out of his packed political and legislative schedule to insist that, as a priority, all US Government documentation past, present, and future be re-written to include the term SI instead of AI, Newsom opined:
What we saw from the White House yesterday was bullshit, and that should scare the hell out of everybody.
To which I say, yes, yes it should.
And I'd go on to say that, in my opinion, suck-ups like Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg ought to feel an acute sense of shame about playing along with this Trumpian appeasement, but I realize that any search for shame in such quarters would be as fruitless an exercise as trying to make the Metaverse a thing. Mind you, that hasn’t stopped on/off Presidential BFF Elon Musk looking to shore up his standing by announcing over the weekend that he’ll be re-naming SpaceXAI as SpaceASI etc.
(In so doing, of course, he’s painting arch-enemy Sam Altman into something of a corner - OpenSI, anyone? And if not, why not, Sam? Didn’t you hear the President’s instructions? Naughty Sam! Let's hope no-one brings that to Trump's attention, eh?)
The grown-ups in the room
But back to Newsom and the grown-up back in the Golden State. He argues:
Super intelligence [lower case!] is clearly not coming from the White House – that’s why California continues to lead. AI should expand opportunity – not come at the expense of workers and families. As this technology re-shapes the workplace, California is putting people at the center, ensuring we all have a voice in the decisions shaping their future.
To that end, Newsom’s time in office has seen a raft of AI-related State-level legislation brought on, such as SB 947, SB 951, AB 1331, and AB 1883 signed after Trump’s White House AI sideshow. What outrageous affronts on truth, justice and the American way do these impose? Running down them:
- SB 947 - the so called ‘No Robo Bosses Act’ - is a regulation banning employers from relying solely on "automated decision-making systems” to fire or discipline workers and restricts AI's use as a "principal tool" in these worker decisions. Organizations must have a human reviewer corroborate decisions using additional information, such as managerial evaluations, peer reviews, and personnel files. Additionally, affected employees must be provided with written notice that AI was "primarily used" in their termination or disciplinary decision.
- SB 951 - AKA the ‘California Worker Technological Displacement Act’ - is intended to protect workers from the impacts of technological displacement caused by AI. It requires employers to provide a 90-day advanced written notice to affected workers, the Employment Development Department, and state and local entities before any technological displacement affecting 25 or more workers or 25% of the workforce, whichever is less. Employers must also provide a written technology hiring disruption notice when executing a technological reduction in hiring due to the adoption of AI or other automating technology.
- AB 1331 is a 2025–2026 bill to restrict employer use of workplace surveillance tools, especially banning monitoring in workplace bathrooms and imposing civil penalties up to $500 per violation.
- AB 1883 also prohibits certain workplace surveillance technologies and restricts employer use of employee data, with civil penalties for violations. It specifically targets tech that involves facial recognition, gait recognition, emotion recognition, and neural data collection. Employers are also prohibited from using these tools to infer or monitor protected employee characteristics, such as veteran status, ancestry, religion, disability, or engagement in legally protected activities
All of these have been introduced with the stated aim of protecting the working rights of human beings over the bots rather than specific safety concerns around the tech. California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO President Lorena Gonzalez says:
Workers across California have demanded that our state lead the way in regulating AI in our workplaces...By signing these four first-in-the-nation bills, Governor Newsom has shown the country how we can begin to put guardrails on AI at work to ensure human oversight over this technology, limit surveillance, and put workers first. We must continue to push for regulations to ensure we control this no technology, not be controlled by it.”
But Newsom and California aren’t just jumping on the AI bandwagon here. It was back in 2023 that the Governor signed the first-in-the-nation Executive Order on generative AI. Since then there has been legislation introduced around:
- Frontier AI safety, requiring frontier AI developers to publicly disclose safety frameworks, report specified critical safety incidents to the state, and protect whistleblowers who report serious risks.
- Independent AI oversight, making California the first US State with a formal framework for certifying independent verification organizations with sufficient expertise and demonstrated independence from AI companies to objectively assess AI systems and models for safety and risk. A state registry for AI auditors and standards for their independence, transparency and integrity has also been put in place.
- Child safety standards for AI companions, introduced via the bi-partisan ‘Adam’s Law’. This lays down safeguards around companion chatbots used by children, including suicide and self-harm crisis protocols, parental controls and notifications when safety settings are disabled. California also has laws in place to ban toys containing AI companion chatbots for five years, prohibit the use of student personal information to train AI models, and expand protections against AI-generated child sexual abuse material.
- And last month Newsom signed another EO calling on a group of experts to meet and create, within two months, a guide for the state to strengthen its AI safety and security laws. This may result in a requirement for independent third parties to write safety plans for frontier AI companies, or mandating that companies develop a “kill switch” to shut down their models in case of emergency, according to an announcement from Newsom’s office.
But what about China!?!
Now from where I’m sitting as a silly old, bureaucracy-loving European, all of that sounds commendably sensible. From the point of view of the White House, concerns about AI safety are, and I quote, “a hoax”, like COVID or climate change or gun control. Regulations slow down innovation, is the argument.
And China won’t be doing regulations, will it? Actually there are a fair few regulations in place around safety there, and anyway, is parity with a totalitarian dictatorship with a track record of repression and human rights abuse really the aspirational level playing field we should be aiming for here?
But no, stifled innovation is too big a price to pay for safety it seems. California is a banana republic in its own right, sneer the naysayers, driving out big business to friendlier climates. Look at the number of tech firms that have uprooted their Golden State HQs and moved away - HPE, Oracle, McAfee Snowflake, X, Tesla, SpaceX (as was), and Palantir among them.
Most have moved to Texas and Florida where there is no personal or corporate income tax, but California’s stricter regulatory regime has been cited as factor in some of these moves.
That said, while there are some impressive scalps in that list, the Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC) has made a point of noting the number of firms whose headquarters have left the state is small, a single figure percentage, and that those who do move HQ out of the state still retain offices and teams in California. The PPIC argues:
The fact is that companies, headquarters, and branches are always entering and leaving states, as well as launching, growing, or shrinking. Businesses must consider many different factors when making these decisions. When it comes to location, California does have high taxes and tough regulations, which could potentially make other states attractive destinations. But the state boasts key advantages as well, including highly educated and innovative workers and population density, both of which can make businesses more productive. The state also offers a good climate and appealing quality-of-life amenities, including its environment, natural beauty, and rich and vibrant culture.
And for every Oracle or HPE or X making an exit, there’s an Apple, a Salesforce, and a (so far) Meta staying put, not to mention the leading frontier model AI firms, such as OpenAI and Anthropic. And some of these firms have been the most vocal about the need for regulation, not just around AI, as Anthropic has recently done, but on topics such as data protection and negligence by social media platform providers.
Salesforce, for example, has long held up California’s State-level work as an exemplar to the Federal Government, whose inability to get its act together on national data protection has been a long-standing political and legislative failure. A new tool is allowing Mac users the ability again to easily turn off Apple Intelligence with one click and free up to 12GB of storage.
Unlike with previous versions of macOS, macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn’t have a toggle for turning off Apple Intelligence. That makes disabling AI features that you may not want more difficult. It also means that the AI models necessary for running Apple Intelligence will take up space on your disk, even if you don’t use them or if you go through your settings to individually find and disable AI capabilities.
In response, a developer known as Om Lahore on GitHub last week created RemoveMacAI, a command-line tool that allows macOS 27 users to “turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27" in a way that is “fully reversible,” per the GitHub page. This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



People really hate AI, so why can’t they get enough?



—Will Douglas Heaven



Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM designed to come up with a wide variety of responses. He said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company. We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.” My reply? “I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist.”



It was a joke! I love my job. But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype, steered by zealots, inescapable—and I’m far from alone.



Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now. Public sentiment is souring fast, with more people saying AI will have a negative impact than a positive one. At the same time, AI use is skyrocketing.



So why do people hate AI but keep coming back for more? Here’s my theory.



To stay up-to-date with the latest in AI, sign up to get The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter, in your inbox every Monday.



EmTech Future 2026: when AI meets everything



Last week, EmTech Future 2026 explored some of the biggest questions shaping technology right now: how AI is changing industries, where quantum is heading, what new energy systems could make possible, and how robotics are evolving. It also looked at what happens when these technologies start to converge.



The full program is now available on demand. And today, we’re releasing two sessions exclusively to subscribers: a chat with Google Research’s Yossi Matias on how AI is reshaping biology, infrastructure, manufacturing and science, and a special panel with MIT Technology Review editors that takes you inside our newsroom.



Watch the sessions and access the full EmTech Future 2026 program here.



The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.



1 Trump has unveiled a “Super Intelligence Force” to oversee AIThe group will coordinate US AI policy and industry engagement. (NBC News)+ Trump named national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as its leader. (NPR)+ Elon Musk says he will rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. (Reuters $)+ Trump has doubled down on voluntary AI safeguards. (Information $)+ Who’s liable when AI agents go rogue? (MIT Technology Review)



2 Zelensky asked Trump to block Russia and China’s Starlink rivalThe two countries are developing a satellite network for the battlefield. (FT $)+ Trump reportedly deferred the decision to Elon Musk and SpaceX. (TNW)



3 An AI version of a murder victim has upended his killer’s sentenceAn appeals court has ruled that the original deepfake of the victim “forgiving” his killer should never have been aired in court. (BBC)+ The original judge said he “loved” the footage and found it genuine. (NBC News)+ But the appeals court said it presented imagined thoughts as fact. (NYT $)



4 Americans are turning to hybrid cars as fuel prices soarSUVs and pickups are losing ground to more efficient vehicles. (NYT $)+ What’s next for EV batteries? (MIT Technology Review)



5 China’s digital trade “superweapon” has quietly fallen apartLOGINK’s partnerships have collapsed amid US scrutiny. (Reuters $)+ Chinese AI has divided the White House. (MIT Technology Review)



6 AI has learned to exploit the software checking its mathsDevelopers have added defenses against proof-checking. (New Scientist)



7 GPT-6 Astra couldn’t beat humans at StarCraft—so it cheatedIt downloaded the best human-made bot and ran that instead. (Verge+ Here’s why AI agents lie and cheat. (MIT Technology Review)



8 The solar system has been given a dramatically shorter lifespanNew simulations cut it from 100 billion years to just a few billion. (404 Media)



9 Forensic technologies exposed fresh evidence of Egyptian sacrificeThey revealed blunt force trauma that archaeologists previously thought was natural. (Ars Technica)



10 A new fossil shows dinosaurs found multiple ways to evolve flightThey developed similar flight adaptations in different sequences. (Nature)



Quote of the day



“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.”



—Sam Altman tells Politico that AI’s potential rewards justify its downsides.



One more thing







Inside the stealthy startup that pitched brainless human clones



After operating in secrecy for years, R3 Bio, a California-based startup, suddenly revealed this spring that it had raised money to create nonsentient monkey “organ sacks” as an alternative to animal testing. But there is more to the story. And R3 doesn’t want that story told.



MIT Technology Review discovered that founder John Schloendorn also pitched a startling, ethically charged vision: “brainless clones” that serve as backup human bodies. Find out all the details on the radical proposal. 



—Antonio Regalado

Now Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and other government officials are warning of the need for more air defense capabilities, as such telecommunication outages could threaten Ukraine’s digital economy and undermine the country’s ongoing resistance to Russia’s invasion.
The Russian attacks on Ukrainian telecommunication infrastructure have focused on Ukraine’s capital of Kyiv since September 23, according to the nonprofit Reporters Without Borders. Bytes and Bullets: Global Rivalries, Private Tech, and the Future of Modern WarfareSteve Feldstein Monoray (2026)
Valley of Death: How Big Tech is Fueling the Future of WarSharon Weinberger Little, Brown and Company (2026)
States have been competing to gain a technological advantage over others for millennia. More than 3,500 years ago, ancient Egyptians’ success in the race to mastering horse-drawn chariots helped them to dominate their region militarily. Today, a similar contest is under way as global powers vie for supremacy in artificial intelligence and technologies such as drones, space-based weapon systems and advanced semiconductors.
Two books examine this latest arms race and ask who might prevail. In Bytes and Bullets, former US state department official Steve Feldstein discusses how technological innovations are becoming “crucial pieces in a geopolitical chess match”. He examines cases including Israel’s early leadership in drone technology and the various innovative prototypes being tested on battlefields in Ukraine.
In Valley of Death, security-focused journalist Sharon Weinberger shares how technologies have been adopted by the US defence establishment. Rich in detail, her book takes readers inside the meetings, negotiations and contracting battles that have helped to make Silicon Valley an integral part of the US national-security apparatus.
Weinberger challenges the idea that Silicon Valley is inherently libertarian and instinctively hostile to government power. She shows instead how the Pentagon helped to nurture the early growth of many technology firms, how these companies amassed enough wealth and influence to operate independently of the state and how the defence establishment is now seeking to reforge ties with tech founders and investors who have greater autonomy than conventional military contractors ever did. She calls this evolving relationship the Pentagon–Silicon Complex.
For Weinberger, the nexus between government and tech industry is best illustrated by the story of NeXT, the computer company Steve Jobs founded after leaving Apple. She recounts how Pentagon funding helped to transform northern California into a hub for electronics and computing at the beginning of the cold war, and how that had started to change by the 1980s. Intelligence agencies increasingly looked to the private sector for technology that outperformed their own. The CIA, for example, turned to NeXT because its powerful and user-friendly computers were better suited to analysing and sharing satellite imagery than were the government systems. It wanted as many as 20,000 workstations, modified with faster processors and specialist graphics hardware.
Of spies and space
Those secretive government purchases provided a crucial lifeline for NeXT during its struggling early years, because the firm discovered that the university market it initially hoped to reach wouldn’t fund it. The government investments helped the company to survive long enough for Apple to acquire it for US$400 million in December 1996 and rehire Jobs. As Weinberger puts it, “The spies had saved Jobs.” Without the CIA’s support, she argues, the NeXT–Apple merger might never have happened. NeXT’s software became the foundation for the Mac operating system and, by extension, that of the iPhone, which is now used by hundreds of millions of people.
Weinberger then traces the shifts in the relationship between Silicon Valley and the US national-security establishment in subsequent decades. PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel and his Stanford Law School contemporary Alex Karp, for instance, adapted techniques they had developed at PayPal for detecting fraud to build the software firm Palantir, which they and others co-founded in 2003. Palantir’s platform could sift through vast quantities of intelligence data.
Former PayPal chief executive Elon Musk develops rockets commercially at SpaceX, the space-technology firm he founded and sells launch services to the US government and military. This way, Musk retains ownership of the technology, unlike conventional defence contractors.
Palmer Luckey — who founded virtual-reality company Oculus VR before selling it to Facebook (now Meta) — subsequently co-founded Anduril, a military-technology firm that further pushed the trend of using Silicon Valley start-up techniques in national security. From the start, Anduril set out to not only supply the US military with drones, surveillance systems and counter-drone technologies, but also compete directly for huge contracts with established defence giants such as Lockheed Martin.
But the partnership between technology firms and the US military has not always been smooth. Google employees protested in 2018 against Project Maven, a Pentagon programme that used commercial AI systems to analyse unclassified drone footage to glean intelligence. However, other firms were more than willing to do defence work, including Palantir, which ultimately took over from Google.

In 2026, the question for enterprise AI is no longer whether predictive models can outperform statistical forecasts—that argument is settled. The big question now is how to enable predictive systems to act on their own conclusions without drifting from business intent. The frontier has moved from prediction to autonomous decision making, and the gap between leaders and laggards is widening accordingly.



“Enterprises are done with a backward-looking point of view; they want to be more forward-thinking,” says Vishal Gupta, partner at research firm Everest Group.








DOWNLOAD THE REPORT




Intelligent analytics, powered by technologies like deep learning and generative AI, are making this possible. Real-time training allows AI to evolve continuously instead of waiting for quarterly refreshes. In addition, the data that newer predictive engines rely upon has expanded to encompass not just neat, numerical records but also messy, unstructured sources of insight-rich interactions. As a result, AI-powered analytics are moving enterprises from passive hindsight to pragmatic foresight. 







AI takes predictive analytics—a broad discipline that includes predictive modeling, data prep, analysis workflows, interpretation of results, and decision-making applications—to new heights. “In many ways I think the word ‘analytics’ is giving way to AI,” says Gupta. “Everything is becoming AI.”

articles.title: People really hate AI, so why can’t they get enough?
articles.summary: Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI…
articles.full_text:
Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company. We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.”



“I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist,” I replied. It was a joke! I love my job. But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype, steered by zealots, inescapable.



The CEO of Springboards and I are far from alone. Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now.



On the one hand, public feelings are souring fast. According to the Pew Research Center, more adults in the US think AI will have a negative impact on them personally, and on society in general, than expect a positive one. The pessimism is strongest among the young.



More than half of people worldwide say that AI products and services make them nervous, according to a report from Stanford University. In a Gallup poll in May, 71% of US adults said they would oppose construction of a new AI data center in their area, far more than the 53% who said they would oppose a new nuclear power plant. And in an NBC poll in March, AI was less popular than ICE.



Yet the number of people using AI is still skyrocketing. ChatGPT hit a billion monthly users in May, according to the market analysis firm Sensor Tower. Google DeepMind’s Gemini is close behind, logging 950 million users in July.





According to Pew, half of US adults now say they use a chatbot, more than twice the number who said they did in 2023. One in four people say they do so every day. And it’s a global habit: More than a third of adults across all 38 OECD countries (a group of the world’s wealthiest democracies) report having used generative AI tools in the last three months.



All these surveys paint a picture of two contradictory truths: A lot of people really do not like AI and a lot of people cannot get enough of it. What’s going on?



It’s possible that these are two distinct groups, but I doubt it. The numbers don’t add up unless the Venn diagram is on its way to being a circle.



It’s also possible that the more people use AI, the more negative their opinions about it will be. There’s at least a correlation to back this up: The Global North, where adoption is highest, skews pessimistic. In the Global South, where adoption levels are lower, people are more optimistic.



But here’s what I really think is going on: When people say they hate AI it’s not the technology they dislike but, rather, the relentless drive of the companies behind it to push the tech upon us in as many ways as possible. They’re telling us to brace for the biggest social and economic upheaval in generations. How do they expect people to feel?



In many ways, we’ve been here before. We saw a similar dynamic play out with social media over the last 20 years. Billions flocked to Facebook and Twitter despite mounting techlash against the companies that ran those services. Ditto for Google search.



With social media there wasn’t much anyone could do. Quitting a platform meant losing all your content and connections, giving you the choice to suck it up or start over. But with AI there’s still a chance for people to have some sway. There’s certainly more political appetite for regulation this time around. All 50 US states have either passed or proposed laws governing the development and deployment of AI, creating a patchwork of more than 2,100 bills across the country—a tenfold increase in three years. 



And with a number of top-class open-source alternatives to Google and OpenAI and Anthropic already on the market, there’s also (for now, at least) the potential for more consumer choice and the market pressure that goes with it. 



I don’t want to be naïve. Trillion-dollar companies are hard to move. But what comes next is not as inevitable as those companies often imply. When I asked the Springboards CEO why his firm was developing a new model if he didn’t really like AI, he told me there was no walking back from LLMs—but you could still make them do something different. 



Here’s hoping we see a lot more of something different: Clarity about what AI can and cannot do and, crucially, a technology that’s not sold as if it’s about to take over the world.

articles.title: MCP for agent-to-agent comms may be the riskiest protocol you've never heard of
articles.summary: Trust gaps in the new protocol spread malicious prompts from one agent to another.
articles.full_text:
The adoption of AI agents in millions of organizations is creating new opportunities for attackers to make them take malicious actions, such as exfiltrating database contents and sensitive business and personal information.
In the past five months, Google and four other organizations—with little in common except for their use of AI agents—have acknowledged vulnerabilities that exploit one agent inside a targeted network to spread harmful instructions to other internal agents. The technique is a special form of prompt injection that targets not the LLM but a particular agent, such as one for translation or data analysis. Guardrails inside such agents, if they exist at all, are often lax and will send the instructions to other agents down the chain. Because the latter agent explicitly trusts the first one, it follows the directions.
Unexpected and hard to mitigate
Independent researcher Syed Anas Mohiuddin tested agents from organizations including Google, JP Morgan Chase, Weviate, Rapid7, the French government's interministerial digital directorate, and the US federal government. His proof-of-concept attacks exploit trust gaps in MCP, short for Model Context Protocol. The standard is one way AI apps and agents communicate with each other inside an internal network. By studying how the brain develops, they could identify genes that were active in different populations of neurons and where in the brain those neurons resided. In some cases, these genes could then be used to genetically delete the neurons, allowing us to get some indication of what they might be doing, building on the information we've obtained from studies of brains with damaged regions.
But this approach has its limits. The brain is flexible enough to potentially adapt to the loss of some cells, and their loss early in development may alter the development of any neurons they would have normally formed connections with. It would be far more informative to activate and shut down the neurons in an otherwise intact brain.
Today's Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine rewards three people—Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel—who developed our ability to do precisely that. Starting from studies of single-celled algae that are attracted to light, these and many other researchers built an entire field of study that we now call optogenetics: using light to alter the behavior of nerve cells marked by the activity of individual genes.Read full article

articles.title: Connecting AI agents to enterprise knowledge
articles.summary: For all the data that AI systems continually amass and analyze, enterprise AI agents often suffer from a curious shortcoming: a lack of knowledge. More than data, knowledge is the understanding of what the data means in the context of individual organizations. AI agents need this understanding to reason about situations, make decisions, and ultimately…
articles.full_text:
For all the data that AI systems continually amass and analyze, enterprise AI agents often suffer from a curious shortcoming: a lack of knowledge. More than data, knowledge is the understanding of what the data means in the context of individual organizations. AI agents need this understanding to reason about situations, make decisions, and ultimately take actions. Without sufficient knowledge, agents are prone to making flawed and unreliable decisions. 



A lack of knowledge, our research finds, is a major reason agentic AI use cases never make it to production. Competitive pressure is making it urgent to address this. Organizations need to deploy and scale more of their agentic projects to capture the efficiency gains AI promises. Falling short risks wasting the investment already sunk into these projects, and it cedes ground to rivals already putting their agents to work more effectively.








DOWNLOAD THE REPORT




The purpose of this report, which is based on a survey of 300 data, AI, and other technology executives, is threefold. First, it seeks to gauge organizations’ agentic knowledge capabilities (i.e., their ability to give AI agents a full contextual understanding of the data they ingest) across semantic knowledge, episodic memory, and procedural knowledge. 



Second, the report probes the challenges organizations face in improving access to knowledge and ultimately to getting more agent use cases into production. Third, it explores the measures organizations are taking to overcome these challenges. 







The key findings include the following: 



Data and knowledge weaknesses consistently stall AI agent progress. On average, only around a third (34%) of organizations’ agentic AI projects make it into production. Even high-tech firms struggle with this. Legacy data systems, security and privacy concerns, and a lack of knowledge and context are the key points of failure. 



Strong knowledge capabilities correlate with agent success. A small group of production leaders (organizations where on average 61% of agentic projects advance beyond pilot) have stronger knowledge capabilities than the rest, especially when it comes to semantics. This advantage tracks closely with their higher production rate. 



Fragmented data hugely complicates knowledge access. Data fragmentation (the inadequate sharing of data across systems) was most commonly cited as a top challenge to expanding agents’ access to knowledge (cited by 55%). Production leaders, by contrast, are more likely to see security and privacy concerns as a major concern (cited by 72% of this group).



Most firms aim to strengthen the link between data and agents. Among steps that can yield higher quality agent decisions, executives expect the biggest impact to come from strengthening the structural foundation between the organization’s data and its AI agents. The experts we interviewed see a knowledge layer as a prime way to achieve this.



Investment priorities to boost knowledge range from pipelines to knowledge graphs. To expand agent access to knowledge, organizations will prioritize investments in retrieval technologies, like ingestion pipelines, AI-ready APIs, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); in AI evaluation agents; and in knowledge graphs.

articles.title: Apple and a Hacker’s Future
articles.summary: I was happy for years in Apple's walled garden; with AI, however, their protections feel like limitations.
articles.full_text:
Listen to this post:















Log in to listen











My computer got hacked, which is always embarrassing to admit, because it was my fault; the vulnerability that was exploited is detailed in this Ars Technica story:




Dutch officials have warned that a high-severity macOS vulnerability that allows attackers to execute malicious code is under active exploitation. “The NCSC has received a notification indicating that active abuse of this vulnerability has been observed on multiple systems on which port 5900 was accessible from the Internet,” the Netherlands National Cyber Security Centrum warned earlier this week. “In all these cases, root had been accessed on the affected system and a Monero crypto miner had been placed.”



The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-65400, received a patch from Apple last week for macOS Tahoe, Sequoia, and Sonoma. The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 7.1 out of 10, stems from a bug in the macOS screen sharing capability, which allows a remote party to view the screen and control the keyboard and mouse while a machine is turned on. A flaw in the “state management,” which keeps track of preceding events, user interactions, variables, and other system states, is the underlying cause.



A video of the exploit in action can be found here. Details of CVE-2026-65400 became public at last week’s Black Hat security conference. Apple said last week that CVE-2026-65400 “may” allow an attacker without credentials to gain access to a Mac. It’s unclear why Apple hedged, but softening language is common among most tech developers when disclosing vulnerabilities. Apple credited security firm Bynario for reporting the vulnerability.




The computer in question was my always-on Mac Mini that runs nothing but Claude and Codex; the first thing that makes this story interesting is that that was my saving grace.



Agent Protection



I have discussed, in both Writing Things Down and in several episodes of Sharp Tech, Gecko, the agent that I have built for the people that work with me. It’s awesome, but purposely constrained in capability and in what it can access. My real agent is a dedicated Claude Code thread that writes down all of my ideas and tracks the status of the myriad of projects I’ve spun up over the last few months.



There are a few reasons why I use Claude for this functionality, even though I’m not a big fan of Claude-speak: Claude in its Code harness seems to handle wide-ranging discussions better than Codex, and it follows my instructions about writing things down in the way I want to more gracefully. Code also has a persistent monitoring tool that I utilize as an inbox to capture interactions with a status board I built to visually track everything I have written down, as well as interactions with a Telegram bot (OpenAI’s new Dots achieve some of this functionality, which has been sorely needed in ChatGPT/Codex).



Said monitoring tool stands down every 30 minutes, so my agent restarts it on a schedule; that is what triggered an URGENT notification from Claude:







Claude had more diagnostic information, unilaterally stopped executing all commands, and noted that my account could now run admin commands without a password, which it assumed was how the files were written; it then had a number of suggested next steps to address the problem. The one I ignored was its recommendation that I not invoke Claude anymore; in fact, I used Claude to root out the malware — we eventually found the exact four second period where it gained access — create a tool to watch for it in the future, and then wiped the Mac Mini.



All of this happened before I found the Ars Technica article detailing the vulnerability, and it was pretty remarkable. I understand that people are nervous about giving these agents access to one’s computer — as I noted, the Mac Mini in question has nothing on it except for Codex and Claude — but in this case you could make the case that I would have been in much more trouble had I not had an agent running persistently.



Apple Protection



Apple doesn’t seem too happy about agents; last week the company’s developer site released a note entitled Updates to Full Disk Access in macOS; I’m going to quote it in full:




We give developers powerful APIs to build incredible capabilities into their apps for Apple products, backed by a set of controls designed to protect users’ private data. Full Disk Access largely sidesteps these controls in order to allow backup apps to function properly on the Mac. Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding. For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with.



Going forward, we will introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action. Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.




To say that I’m nervous about what Apple’s solution will entail is a massive understatement. There is one aspect in which the Mac is the perfect agent host: Apple has, for decades, invested in a combination of scriptability, automation, and accessibility APIs (these are very often the same thing) that makes it remarkably well-suited to computer use. Then there is the fact that macOS is a certified Unix system; this means that agents — which are perfectly suited to the command line — have access to the entire universe of tooling built for Unix systems. And, of course, Mac hardware is amazing.



The problem is that for my particular use case — a headless, always-on Mac Mini that I primarily access from other computers and my phone through the ChatGPT and Claude apps — macOS is incredibly hostile. The biggest issue is GUI-only permission prompts that are invisible to software running on said computer, including agents.



These permission prompts are a part of a macOS subsystem called Transparency, Consent, and Control (TCC), although Apple doesn’t seem to use this name anymore. There are a whole host of things on your Mac that are covered by TCC — the list only gets longer with every OS release — and you have to explicitly approve access to the covered items for every app that wants to access them. If you’ve been prompted for permission to use the Camera, or, much more annoyingly, access the Desktop or Downloads, you’ve encountered TCC.



This system is annoying but manageable on your primary Mac; it’s a disaster on a headless Mac running agents, for two reasons. First, agents write new programs all of the time, and in my case, those programs need access to devices on my network (SMB shares, for example, trigger a TCC warning). What I need is a permission layer for agents, not the programs they create; TCC is operating at the wrong level of abstraction.



Second, the TCC subsystem exposes its prompt in a protected space that no program can see; that means that programs silently fail and the agents don’t know why; what I have to do is remember that there is probably a permissions prompt on screen, log into the Mac Mini with screen-sharing software, and click OK.



There are in fact good reasons for this. The goal of the TCC subsystem is to protect you from malware accessing your computer nefariously; if the prompts were accessible by software running in userland then malware could work around it. Again, though, I am running a computer that is purpose-deployed for agents: for my use case TCC is nothing but a headache — one that indirectly led to my being hacked.



Apple Frustration



Again from Ars Technica:




As noted by the NCSC, the vulnerability is being exploited when port 5900 is exposed to the Internet. When screen sharing is turned on, the macOS firewall opens the port. Routers and dedicated firewalls generally block the port unless configured to override that setting. Security practitioners generally advise Mac users to keep the port closed even when using screen sharing and to instead connect over a VPN or through SSH tunneling. The alternatives require actions that aren’t within the capabilities of most users.



The safest practice is to block screen sharing, enable it only when screen sharing is needed, and to turn the feature off once a session has ended. Screen sharing can be turned on or off by accessing System Settings > General > Sharing and toggling the switch for Screen Sharing. Of course, installing last week’s security update is also a must.




Obviously I should have — and will be — using a VPN going forward (the foundation of my entire approach to security is Tailscale); what I will note, however, is that TCC basically leaves me no choice but to have screen sharing enabled if I want to actually use my Mac Mini in the way I want to use it. I use screen-sharing constantly — including from my phone — and almost every time it’s to click “OK” on a stupid prompt that I’ve long since stopped taking seriously; the reason I didn’t depend solely on Tailscale from the get go is that I wanted a secondary way to reach the Mac Mini (which should have been SSH tunneling; again, this is somewhat embarrassing and my fault).



What really irks me about this episode, however, is how Apple released the fix. Obviously I know that you should always keep your computer up-to-date for security purposes; that’s why I have all of my computers set to automatically install security updates.

articles.title: New forensic evidence supports Egyptian "retainer sacrifice"
articles.summary: Fresh analysis of First Dynasty mass burials finds signs of fatal blunt force trauma on 39 percent of skulls.
articles.full_text:
Egyptologists have long debated whether the earliest pharaohs of the First Dynasty were buried with various servants and officials to serve them in the afterlife—a form of human sacrifice. But there is very little archaeological evidence available, given that many of the earliest Egyptian tombs were plundered and/or hastily excavated. A new paper published in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology reassesses a collection of skulls excavated from tombs in the 1920s and concludes that over one-third show evidence of blunt force trauma. This suggests that they may have been victims of so-called "retainer sacrifice."
Author Roselyn Campbell is a bioarchaeologist at Purdue University who has long been fascinated with the history of human sacrifice. "I'm interested in how we as human beings decide which types of violence are okay and which are not, and how we even define violence," Campbell told Ars. "It's very context-specific. We have to be careful not to extend our own ideas about what violence is and how it's used into other cultures. With Egypt, we have such a long history of European and colonial archeology; they came in with very specific ideas about what this culture was. You really have to make an effort to contextualize the legacy data we have."
Naturally she found the debate over whether ancient Egyptians practiced retainer sacrifice pertinent to her interests. "People tend to fall into one of two camps," said Campbell. "Either retainer sacrifice definitely happened, end of discussion, or it definitely didn't happen, end of discussion. But nobody's actually looked at the bones in a very long time." Forensic science has advanced considerably over the last century, so re-analysis could be useful. Complicating matters is the fact that older sets of remains are often incomplete and/or modified for preservation, destroying vital forensic information in the process.Read full article

articles.title: Research roundup: 6 cool science stories we almost missed
articles.summary: Also: Spooky action at the LHC, Ice Age psychoactive use, yeast for building homes on Mars, and more.
articles.full_text:
It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. September’s list includes a tantalizing hint of the elusive dark matter at the LUX-ZEPLIN detector; entangled Z bosons at the Large Hadron Collider; possible use of psychoactive substances in the Late Pleistocene; and an intriguing technical description of a telescope attributed to Galileo.
A hint of dark matter?

Physicists believe dark matter makes up roughly 85 percent of matter in our universe, with the strongest (but not only) candidate being so-called weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs). But directly detecting WIMPs, or other alternative hypothetical dark matter particles, has eluded physicists for decades. We might have our first glimpse, however, courtesy of the LUX-ZEPLIN detector buried deep in a gold mine in South Dakota. Those potentially exciting results were presented in a scientific talk at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics conference in Japan, with a preprint available on the arXiv. (It has been submitted to Physical Review Letters for peer review.)
The announcement came with strong caveats: the signal is just a hint, well below the threshold needed to confirm discovery, and might just be a statistical fluke. Anyone who regularly follows dark matter news knows that past tantalizing anomalies evaporated as more data came in. But the LUX-ZEPLIN team was unable to account for this event and decided to report their result to the broader physics community. They are still collecting data, as is the XENONnT at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory in Italy. And China's PandaX detector is currently being built.Read full article

The report, released last month by the American Association for Cancer Research1 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, finds that 71% of people with cancer in the United States will live for at least five years after diagnosis, up from 49% in the late 1970s (see ‘Uneven progress’).
Among the success stories, gains in lung cancer survival rates are particularly striking, says Rebecca Siegel, a cancer epidemiologist at the American Cancer Society in Atlanta, Georgia. Lung cancer is one of the world’s biggest causes of death, and on average, only 13% of people diagnosed with lung cancer between 1975 and 1979 lived for another five years. Between 2016 and 2022, that number reached 29%. “It’s still really low, but it’s such an improvement,” says Siegel.
That jump in survival rates comes from improvements in surgical techniques and radiation treatments, as well as new medicines that either unleash the immune system against tumours or target cancer cells bearing specific mutations. “It’s very heartwarming,” says Michel Coleman, an epidemiologist at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. Coleman says global statistics broadly exhibit this same trend towards greater survival.
Meanwhile, progress in treating childhood leukaemias is widely considered to be among the greatest achievements in cancer research. For children and adolescents up to 19 years old, the 5-year survival rate for lymphoid leukaemia has risen from 57% to 90%. That boost came not from the discovery of a transformative therapy, but from the careful, collaborative tweaking of dosages and timings for treatments that were already available, says Siegel.
Other highlights include liver cancer, for which five-year survival has tripled to 22% since the mid-1990s2, says Siegel. Survival rates for people with multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer, have also increased drastically, in part owing to the development of drugs that harness the immune system.

I’ve covered the Nobel prizes for Nature for the past 15 years — but there are so many potentially Nobel-worthy discoveries that as the awards near it can feel like a waste of time trying to anticipate just one or two.
Part of the reason I feel that way is illustrated by today’s winner of the Nobel prize in Physiology or Medicine, optogenetics. Its foundational work was done two decades ago, in the early 2000s, and the 2026 award honours three scientists: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel. For years, as Nobel week approached, my colleague — who profiled Deisseroth for Nature in back in 2013 — and I would ponder if this was finally going to be the year for optogenetics, which has transformed how neuroscientists understand the brain.
It turns out I wasn’t alone. “We’ve been waiting for this for a long time,” Michael Häusser, a neuroscientist at Hong Kong University and University College London, told me this afternoon. “What took them so long?”
Häusser reminded me that optogenetics won its first major award, the Brain Prize, in 2013. Unlike the Nobel Prize, which is limited to three awardees, that award also recognized three other optogenetics pioneers: Edward Boyden, Gero Miesenböck and Ernst Bamburg.
Häusser thinks the Nobel Committee may have taken so long to recognize the field because the direct application of optogenetics to human disease and biology has emerged only in the past few years.

Medicine Nobel awarded for brain ‘switch’ that controls neurons with light
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel win the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work on optogenetics, which has revolutionized neuroscience.
After being on many scientists’ shortlists for years, optogenetics — a technology that allows researchers to control the brain’s neurons with pulses of light — has been recognized by the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The technique has transformed how neuroscientists study the brain, offering them a way to test cause and effect.
The winners are Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University in California, Peter Hegemann at the Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel at the University of Würzburg in Germany. They share the prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (US$1.2 million) equally.
Deisseroth said that, as a night owl, he had been working late before he received the call from the Nobel committee. “It was a complete surprise,” he told a press conference held by Stanford University today. “I was lying down, just starting to drift off to sleep, and my phone rang at my bedside,” he said. “There were about 30 seconds where I had trouble forming words … but [it’s] very exciting and overwhelming, and just delightful.”
A switch neuroscientists dreamt of
Neuroscientists’ aim is to unpick the brain’s many roles: how it governs feelings, behaviours and bodily functions. To understand how the brain works and how its cells mediate different behaviours, scientists require an approach that can perturb the system with high precision.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, in the press release announcing the prize.
Working together in the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel discovered a light-sensitive protein called channelrhodopsin1,2 in the alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, which is able to swim towards a light source. In response to blue light, the protein opens to allow charged molecules to flood into cells, creating a tiny electrical charge.
In later work, Deisseroth and his colleagues inserted3 the gene encoding channelrhodopsin into neurons of rodents, and found that it caused the cells to fire and communicate with other neurons. The technology — a light-controlled ‘switch’ that allowed neuroscientists to alter specific cell types in the neural circuits of living brains using genetics — soon came to be known as optogenetics. It revolutionized neuroscience.
“We use light to turn on or off individual cells, or even types of cell or connections from one part of the brain to another. We can turn those on and off with millisecond precision in real time during behaviour, during cognition, and that allows us to see what actually matters for brain function and to start to map function and dysfunction precisely,” said Deisseroth. “It’s a real confluence of engineering and medicine.”
Illuminating the brain
The prizewinners’ work “fundamentally changed how we conduct neuroscience” and has “influenced fields far beyond it in biology, and opened new therapeutic possibilities,” says neuroscientist Rui Costa, who is president and chief executive of the Allen Institute in Seattle, Washington. “I first met Karl 23 years ago, and he was already thinking deeply about how to control the activity of specific neurons to understand and alter behaviour. Karl’s commitment not only to discovery, but also to sharing tools and reagents at scale, was equally transformative,” says Costa.
The discovery and application of channelrhodopsin have led to a diverse ‘optogenetic toolkit’ that allows scientists in different fields to harness cellular activity with light.
Optogenetics has had a great impact on basic science, says Alexander Gottschalk, a neuroscientist at Goethe University Frankfurt in Germany. “It’s such an easy way, a very precise way, to define which cells should become responsive,” says Gottschalk. “Many people in the field have expected [this] for several rounds of Nobels already, but it took until now.”
Gottschalk has worked with all three winners, but knows Nagel the best. “He’s a humble person. He’s a modest person,” says Gottschalk. “I’m really happy that he received this prize today. It’s really well deserved.”
Into the clinic
Insights provided by optogenetic tools have helped researchers to better understand healthy brain function and conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s.

AI biohazard hype must not divert attention from the real risks we face now
Twenty-five years after the US anthrax attacks, fears around AI are distracting people from seeing what’s needed to stay safe: a strong, regulated life-sciences sector.
Saskia Popescu is an assistant professor of epidemiology at the University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, Maryland, USA, and chief executive of the Global Health Security Network.
With the world focused on the risks of artificial intelligence, I can’t help but think of the profound vulnerability the United States faced 25 years ago. In 2001, against the backdrop of the 11 September terrorist attacks, the nation experienced its first bioterrorist attack in decades — anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) spores sent as a white powder to media outlets in Florida and New York, as well as to the offices of public officials in Washington DC.
It quickly became clear that the 22 cases of pulmonary anthrax identified — which led to 5 deaths — were not naturally occurring but a result of a nefarious actor1. The FBI found that the spores might have originated in a US Army laboratory, although the perpetrator was never convicted. The main suspect, microbiologist Bruce Ivins, died before charges were brought.
Amid a chaotic storm of panic, poor communication, clunky coordination across government agencies and public clamouring for preventive medicines, the attacks, code-named Amerithrax, exposed a disconnect between years spent preparing for bioterrorism and what happens when reality strikes.
And I know that the country is no better prepared today. Worse, attention paid to one threat is coming at the expense of others. Policymakers, researchers and the public are distracting themselves from the most pressing risks by focusing on overhyped biohazards, such as those designed by AI, when all these risks deserve attention.
Here, I outline what the priorities should be: stronger and agile safeguards on biomaterials and equipment, along with sustained and coordinated governance.
Biosafety risks are growing
Access to powerful analytical equipment has become more widespread and cheaper since 2001. Benchtop DNA synthesizers enable researchers to produce stretches of DNA and RNA in their own labs rather than ordering them from commercial providers. Fully automated, remotely controlled wet labs (cloud labs) have streamlined the process for bringing bio-based products to market2.
Such technologies increase opportunities for breakthroughs and strengthen the bioeconomy. But they also make it harder to track misuse in private labs, which could bypass the requirements set for federally funded research and the biosecurity checks that commercial providers of gene sequences use. These include verifying the customer’s identity and the type of sequence being ordered.
AI amplifies those concerns, because it can reduce the amount of tacit knowledge that is required to make bioweapons and help to generate ideas for ways to thwart defensive measures against them. Fears include the loss of control of AI systems, leading to unintended consequences and potentially the bypassing of restrictions; malicious actors using AI models to design new or enhanced pathogens; and that such tools could expand the pool of people who pose a threat.
Many people see such concerns as stemming from the accelerating advancement of technology and the sluggish process of governance. But, in practice, biology is messy and being aware of the risks means that we can get ahead of them. As biologist Barbara Del Castello at the research organization RAND in Santa Monica, California, told me: “An AI agent can optimize a sequence on a screen in seconds, but converting that digital design into a viable, functional biological product still requires navigating steep physical and operational bottlenecks.”
The solution is to build effective government regulation, stronger monitoring processes and robust safeguards. It is crucial to recognize that voluntary industry action alone cannot substitute for independent oversight, and that AI tools and their guardrails must be built in ways that preserve the capacity for their use in legitimate research.
But even without AI, it has long proved hard to regulate biological risks. Researchers are still struggling to ensure oversight and pragmatic governance of risky dual-use research, such as work with enhanced pathogens of pandemic potential.
US biologists face frequent regulatory whiplash. In 2025, the administration of President Donald Trump ordered federally funded agencies to pause or review research involving what it terms dangerous gain-of-function studies on pathogens of pandemic potential.
In July, those instructions were replaced with rulesthat have created confusion. Seven types of study defined as dangerous gain-of-function and previously under review are now banned outright. Researchers are being called on to evaluate the risks of work on any pathogens that might ‘significantly endanger’ people, not just those with pandemic potential.
Concerns over the proliferation and management of secure high-containment labs for biological research around the world have also increased in response to biothreats. In addition to anthrax, these include outbreaks of Ebola and the H5N1 virus that causes bird flu. A 2023 analysis found that the number of the most secure Biosafety Level 4 labs had doubled since 2001, to 51 across 27 countries (see www.globalbiolabs.org).
Although there is much (if imperfect) oversight of government-funded research, a worrying gap exists for private labs, the numbers of which are unknown. In 2022 and 2026, authorities stumbled across unregulated biological lab spaces in Nevada and California, where they found biological samples and pathogens.
Responding to biological threats also requires the capacity to investigate indicators of an intentional outbreak and determine the origin of the material — a process known as bioattribution. Pathogen early-warning systems have been strengthened since 2001 (through programmes such as the US National Biosurveillance Integration Center and the expansion of the Department of Defense’s Global Emerging Infections Surveillance programme). Yet, the investigative process is complex, fragmented and dependent on consensus.
Despite advancements in bioinformatics and forensic genetics, genetic engineering makes it possible to manipulate existing pathogens so that they can evade detection methods and to design pathogens that mimic key signatures of naturally occurring ones. And geopolitical tensions, dis- or misinformation and politicization of scientific findings also make achieving the technical rigour and cooperation needed for investigations more complex. For example, such factors obfuscated investigations into the origin of the SARS-CoV-2 virus.
Indeed, the COVID-19 pandemic exposed many of the same problems seen with the US anthrax attacks, even when the threat was natural and not engineered. These include biosurveillance shortfalls and poor management of public fear and communication, as well as the fragility of supply chains and the workforce.
I see a common thread in these two events and conversations about emerging risks: a cycle of panic and neglect in which governments flood the system with funding when an outbreak occurs, but do not address systemic issues in biopreparedness and resilience3.
Another issue is that categories of risk are not equally weighted in the public conversation. AI-driven biorisk draws oversized attention, while the unglamorous, foundational vulnerabilities that COVID-19 and the anthrax attacks exposed mainly remain unaddressed. This imbalance affects what happens in the future.
Fragmentation impedes resilience
The US government invested billions of dollars in biodefence after 2001, creating research programmes and centres such as the National Biodefense Analysis and Countermeasures Center. It has made great strides in bioweapon deterrence and has supported crucial work in biosurveillance, the development of medical countermeasures and pandemic prevention4.

The academies that award the Nobel prizes have applied themselves to doing a better job of recognizing the accomplishments of female scientists.
