News
Fossil hints that flight wasn’t linear
The discovery of a complete fossil of a feathered dinosaur species adds to evidence that birds evolved the ability to fly several times rather than through a single lineage. The newly described species belongs to a group of dinosaurs called microraptorines, which are closely related to birds. Researchers found that several flight-related adaptations in microraptorines also evolved in the bird lineage Avialae. But these adaptations did not develop in the same order in the two groups and “thus could not be considered the expression of a shared developmental regime”, the researchers write.
Reference: Nature Communications paper
Can cancer be stopped before it starts?
Cancer researchers are excited about ‘cancer interception’ — a technique in which people at high risk are treated to prevent cancer from ever developing. A combination of early-detection techniques and interception in pancreatic cancer is “going to be the breakthrough strategy that really changes survival”, says surgeon and researcher Diane Simeone. The approval of the landmark pancreatic-cancer drug daraxonrasib (Rasonque), which disarms cancer-causing proteins, could be key to an interception approach.
AI lingo earns a spot in the dictionary
‘Agentic’ and ‘vibe coding’ are among a slew of terms about artificial intelligence that have been added to the online version of the venerable Merriam-Webster dictionary. The entries, which also include tech phrases such as ‘prompt engineering’, are notable for the advanced knowledge needed to understand them, say scholars. “This particular batch, more than any other that I’ve seen, really does feel like it’s a meta-commentary on language,” says Peter Sokolowski, a lexicographer at Merriam-Webster. The sophistication of these entries reflects non-specialists’ expanded access to highly technical terms, he says.
Anthropocene or not-pocene?
‘Anthropocene’ has become useful shorthand for humanity’s footprint on Earth — we even have a Briefing newsletter named after it. But it’s not an official geological epoch, after the idea was rejected in 2024. Now, some scholars say that there are unpublished documents showing that the proposal’s rejection was illegitimate, and that the rationale for the decision was never adequately explained. Researchers involved in the vote maintain that the process was fair and point to a technical explanation for the proposal’s rejection published last month in an issue of Nature Reviews Earth & Environment that focused on the debate.
Reference: Nature Reviews Earth & Environment comment or read the whole focus issue
Features & opinion
How to counter hate without fuelling it
“If you see hate speech online, take it almost as your duty to disagree,” says psychologist Mirta Galesic. “Just say ‘I disagree’. Don’t feel pressured to have an elaborate argument.” The goal, she says, is to highlight widespread, moderate social norms — so ask your friends to chime in and disagree, too. That advice is the result of research including an analysis of more than a million Twitter/X posts made between 2015 and 2018. It found that excessive arguing, getting hostile, or using ‘us-versus-them’ rhetoric only drives toxicity.
Reference: PNAS Nexus paper
Futures: science fiction from Nature
A tired scientist exchanges illuminating messages with himself in The buck stops with me and a man tries to dodge a loaded question in Von Neumann’s party.
Nature | 5 min read & Nature | 6 min read
Podcast: butterflies’ patterns trick the eye
The bright and intricate patterns on butterflies might serve to create visual illusions that baffle birds. By analysing slowed-down videos of butterflies taking off, researchers found that the insect’s markings can create the appearance of movement in one direction, when in fact they’re going the other. “I thought initially, ‘Oh no, I’ve made an error, my code’s gone wrong’,” says visual ecologist Jolyon Troscianko of when he first spotted the butterflies’ deception. “So, I did a lot of double-checking and, no, it was true.”

Release: pwasm 0.2a0
        pwasm is one of my folly projects - an entirely vibe-coded pure Python WebAssembly engine that I built in January during my first bout of AI mania.
I hadn't touched it since January, so I decided to let Claude Opus 5.5 loose on it and see if it could make any significant improvements:

Evaluate current state of pwasm - then consider what it would take to get the MicroPython and micro JavaScript experiments from the research repo working under it - and what it would take to speed it up

42 commits later (with minimal follow-up prompting) it now handles almost all of the WASM specification, and the wheel from PyPI bundles working WASM builds of  MicroPython, QuickJS and Micro QuickJS.
I wouldn't trust this thing at all - hence the alpha version tag - but it's interesting seeing how today's models can improve on the work of models from 10 months ago.

articles.title: Daily briefing: The sky as you’ve never seen it — the month’s best science images
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03141-9Coloured stripes across the sky and a crab caught in jellyfish tentacles are among this month’s sharpest science shots. Plus, a ‘speech clock’ could determine how fast you’re ageing and how invasive plant species are displacing farmers in Africa.
articles.full_text:
Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.
The month’s best science images
This psychedelic snap, titled Botswana Star Trail, was this year’s winner in the Skyscapes category of the ZWO Astronomy Photographer of the Year competition. Photographer Stefano Pellegrini stacked up 340 separate exposures from an August night in 2025 to reveal the sky’s motion over the country’s Nxai Pan National Park from under a canopy of baobab trees (Adansonia spp.).
See more of the month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature’s photo team.
Hidden mark could out AI-made proteins
A watermarking system developed by researchers at Google DeepMind could soon be used to indicate proteins that have been designed by artificial intelligence. This hidden signature involves weaving a faint statistical tell into both the amino-acid sequence and 3D shape of computer-designed proteins — without noticeably compromising their function. The approach could distinguish AI-generated proteins from their natural counterparts in biological databases. But this molecular stamp is removable, meaning that it’s best viewed as one tool in a layered framework for guarding against biological threats, says biosecurity researcher Tessa Alexanian.
‘Speech clock’ tracks ageing in your voice
Scientists have developed a ‘speech clock’ that can predict how well a person is ageing based on their vocal characteristics, such as pitch and talking speed. The team used the clock to calculate the ‘speech age gap’ of individuals: the difference between their age as predicted by the speech clock and their chronological age. Larger gaps were associated with cognitive issues, such as those associated with dementia, which suggests the tool could be used to determine whether a person is ageing faster than expected.
Reference: Science Advances paper
Mouse trial offers hope for endometriosis
A tweaked form of niclosamide, a drug used to treat parasitic infections, has eased some of the symptoms of the chronic condition endometriosis in mice. Researchers gave the modified drug to mice that had been prompted to grow endometrial-like lesions and found that the animals’ sensitivity to pain decreased. The mice also developed fewer and smaller lesions, and had fewer disease-causing macrophages than did mice not given the drug. If replicated in people, the results could provide a “breakthrough” in endometriosis treatment, says reproductive biologist and study co-author Kanako Hayashi.
Reference: Advanced Healthcare Materials paper
Image of the week
Last month, this video took home the top prize at this year’s Small World in Motion competition — and was featured as an Image of the Week in this newsletter. But some researchers have raised concerns that the clip depicts features that are biologically implausible and might have been hallucinated by an artificial-intelligence tool. Optical engineer Ning Xu, who won the competition, wrote on LinkedIn that AI was not used to generate any imagery, but was used in post-production to enhance the image, adding colour to clearly distinguish between structures of similar appearance. (Nature | 5 min read) (Ning Xu/Nikon Small World)
Features & opinion
Invasive plants force farmers to uproot
In central Kenya, the spread of the invasive prickly pear cactus (Opuntia stricta) is forcing pastoralists to move in search of habitable land for their livestock. In Uganda, farmers face a similar struggle with lantana (Lantana camara), or kayukiyuki. The disruption that invasive plant species cause across Africa can build gradually, researchers say, bolstered by factors such as drought and poverty. But efforts to eradicate the plants once they’ve taken hold are often expensive and unrealistic, and their role in displacement receives little attention.
Tuberculosis requires more than new drugs
The treatment of tuberculosis (TB) can’t advance on the promise of new drugs alone, argues epidemiologist Ana Cehovin. Researchers should simultaneously work to understand how to preserve those we already have before resistance renders them useless. For TB drugs to have a lasting impact, scientists should combine genomic and clinical evidence to better understand how resistance might be or already is emerging, who is most at risk and how quickly we need to change course. “This evidence generation must all come as part of the innovation process, not after,” Cehovin writes.
The ties that bind the world are underwater
“We assume the cloud is in the sky,” security expert Elisabeth Braw writes in her new book, “but it’s underwater.” The security expert is talking about the “undersea spaghetti bowl” of communication cables that connects global internet traffic — all of it surprisingly vulnerable. These cables are just one aspect of the underwater infrastructure that supports our civilization, Braw says — much of which is maintained by a system of international trust that is now under threat.
